sources.title: Selected Activities of the Eastgate Neighborhood House, Port Calloway, 1891-1897
sources.attribution: Compiled from the annual reports of the Eastgate Neighborhood House, a settlement opened in 1890 by a group of young college-educated women in the river wards of the fictional industrial city of Port Calloway; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of 1890s settlement house annual reports)
sources.body: The table reports yearly or weekly figures for six activities and conditions recorded by a fictional urban settlement house during the 1890s. The public bath opened in 1893, and the household survey began in 1893.

rows: Adults enrolled in evening English-language classes (per year)
Visits to the public bath (average per week)
Households visited for the sanitation and child labor survey (per year)
Attendance at Sunday Bible class (average per week)
Foreign-born share of the ward population (percent)

items.stem: The activities recorded in the table best illustrate which of the following developments of the late nineteenth century?

options.text: Reformers shaped by the Social Gospel tried to apply Christian ethics to city problems by offering practical services to the urban poor.
options.label: key
options.why: Settlement houses, influenced by Social Gospel ideals, emphasized kindergartens, English classes, baths, and social investigation; the table shows these services expanding while religious instruction stayed small.

options.text: Supporters of Social Darwinism argued that charity interfered with natural competition and that the poor should rely on their own efforts.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Social Darwinists such as followers of Herbert Spencer opposed organized aid to the poor, the opposite of what the settlement's expanding services represent.

options.text: Urban political machines gained the loyalty of immigrant voters by trading jobs, food, and favors for votes at election time.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Machines did aid immigrants, but the table records a reform settlement's programs, not partisan patronage exchanged for votes.

options.text: Farmers formed Grange chapters and cooperatives to share knowledge and challenge the railroads and grain elevator owners.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Granger movement addressed rural economic grievances, not services in an immigrant urban ward.

facts: The Social Gospel movement of the late nineteenth century called on Christians to address social problems such as urban poverty.
Settlement houses such as Hull House, founded in Chicago in 1889, offered kindergartens, classes, and other services to immigrant neighborhoods.

items.stem: Which of the following claims about the Eastgate Neighborhood House is best supported by the data in the table?

options.text: Its practical services grew rapidly in the 1890s, while attendance at its religious instruction stayed nearly unchanged.
options.label: key
options.why: English-class enrollment rose from 60 to 480 (700 percent) and survey visits rose sharply, while Bible class attendance went only from 55 to 58.

options.text: It lost the support of its neighbors after the bath house opened, because immigrant families stopped sending children to classes.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Kindergarten enrollment rose from 40 to 210 after the bath opened; nothing in the data suggests a loss of support.

options.text: It gave up religious activity entirely by 1897 so that it could focus on teaching English and inspecting factories.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Bible class still drew about 58 people a week in 1897, so religious activity did not end.

options.text: Its programs reduced the number of immigrants in the ward, since the foreign-born share fell as English classes grew.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The foreign-born share actually rose from 52 to 63 percent over the period.

facts: Settlement houses in the 1890s offered English-language and citizenship classes to immigrant adults.

items.stem: The changes in the ward's population shown in the table most directly reflect which of the following historical contexts?

options.text: Large numbers of immigrants, increasingly from southern and eastern Europe, settled in crowded industrial cities in the late 1800s.
options.label: key
options.why: The New Immigration of the 1880s and 1890s brought millions of Italians, Poles, Jews, and others into urban tenement districts, matching the rising foreign-born share.

options.text: Large numbers of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities seeking factory jobs during and after the First World War.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Migration began around 1915, after the years covered in the table, and it involved native-born migrants rather than the foreign-born.

options.text: Large numbers of Chinese laborers arrived in western cities to build railroads and work in mining camps in the 1890s.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Chinese immigration had been largely barred since the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, so it cannot explain growth in the 1890s.

options.text: Families left farms on the Great Plains for cities after drought and dust storms ruined their crops.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dust Bowl migration took place in the 1930s and involved native-born farm families.

facts: In the 1880s and 1890s, a growing share of immigrants to the United States came from southern and eastern Europe.
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred most Chinese laborers from entering the United States.

derived.desc: Change in foreign-born share of ward population, 1891 to 1897 (percentage points)

items.stem: Activities like the household survey in the table most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the early twentieth century?

options.text: Progressive campaigns for state laws limiting child labor and setting housing and sanitation standards in cities
options.label: key
options.why: Settlement workers' investigations of tenement and working conditions supplied evidence for Progressive Era child labor laws and tenement reform.

options.text: Congressional passage of quota laws in the 1920s that sharply restricted immigration from southern and eastern Europe
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The quota laws of 1921 and 1924 grew out of nativist pressure; settlement surveys of tenements did not produce immigration restriction.

options.text: Federal programs in the 1930s that paid farmers to reduce crop production in order to raise agricultural prices
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Agricultural Adjustment Act addressed farm prices during the Depression, not urban social conditions documented by settlements.

options.text: Government raids on suspected radicals and deportation of foreign-born activists after the First World War
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Palmer Raids of 1919-1920 came out of the Red Scare, not out of settlement workers' social investigations.

facts: Settlement house residents conducted social surveys of urban neighborhoods in the 1890s and early 1900s.
During the Progressive Era (about 1890-1920), many states passed laws limiting child labor and regulating tenement housing.

input.title: A Connecticut Veteran on the Muskingum, 1789

sources.title: Letter from the Ohio Country
sources.attribution: Letter from Asa Thorne, a former Continental Army sergeant who settled near Marietta on the Muskingum River, to his brother in Windham, Connecticut, 1789 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a frontier settler's family letter)
sources.body: Brother, you ask whether I regret selling the farm at Windham. I do not. Here the land is surveyed into square townships before any man may buy, so no neighbor's crooked fence can steal a rod from me, and one lot in every township is set aside to support a school. Congress has pledged that this country shall not stay a dependency forever. When our numbers are large enough we shall choose our own assembly, and in time we shall enter the Union as a state equal to Connecticut herself. No man here may hold another in bondage. That pleases our deacon, and it keeps out the great planters who would buy up all the bottomlands. My one fear is the Shawnee and Miami towns to the west, whose chiefs say they never sold this ground. The handful of soldiers at the fort cannot guard every cabin, and I pray the new government under the Constitution will do better than the old Congress did.

items.stem: The author's point of view in the excerpt is best described as that of

options.text: a New England migrant who saw federal territorial policy as offering secure landownership and eventual political equality
options.label: key
options.why: Thorne praises the surveyed townships, the school lots, and the promise of statehood on equal terms with Connecticut. This fits a Northeastern veteran who moved west under the Ordinances of 1785 and 1787.

options.text: a Southern land speculator hoping to open the Ohio Valley to plantation agriculture and enslaved labor
options.label: reversal
options.why: Thorne welcomes the ban on slavery because it keeps planters out. That is the opposite of this view.

options.text: an Antifederalist who feared that a stronger central government would threaten the liberties of western settlers
options.label: reversal
options.why: Thorne hopes the new government under the Constitution will protect settlers better than the old Congress did. That is a pro-federal hope, not an Antifederalist fear.

options.text: a supporter of the Western Confederacy who believed that earlier treaties had unjustly taken American Indian land
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Thorne reports the Shawnee and Miami claims but treats them as a threat to his cabin. He does not defend them.

facts: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 provided for territorial government and eventual admission of new states on an equal footing with the original states.
Marietta, founded in 1788 by the Ohio Company of Associates, many of them New England Revolutionary War veterans, was the first permanent American settlement in the Northwest Territory.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the author's concern about the federal government's ability to protect settlers in the Northwest Territory?

options.text: The defeat of Arthur St. Clair's army by a confederation of American Indian nations in 1791
options.label: key
options.why: Warriors led by Little Turtle and Blue Jacket destroyed much of St. Clair's force in 1791. This showed that federal troops could not secure the territory and supports Thorne's fear.

options.text: The Treaty of Greenville, in which American Indian nations ceded much of present-day Ohio in 1795
options.label: reversal
options.why: Greenville followed the American victory at Fallen Timbers. It shows federal power succeeding, so it would weaken the concern rather than support it.

options.text: Shays' Rebellion, in which indebted Massachusetts farmers closed courts and the Confederation could not respond
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Shays' Rebellion did expose the Confederation's weakness. But it was a debtor uprising in New England, not a problem of frontier defense against American Indian nations.

options.text: The Proclamation of 1763, which barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Proclamation was a British policy from before independence. It says nothing about how well the United States government could protect settlers.

facts: In 1791 a Western Confederacy of American Indian nations led by Little Turtle and Blue Jacket defeated U.S. forces under Arthur St. Clair.
The Treaty of Greenville (1795), signed after the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), ceded much of present-day Ohio to the United States.

items.stem: The territorial policies the author describes are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: The Confederation Congress organizing western lands that states had ceded, among its few lasting achievements under the Articles
options.label: key
options.why: The Land Ordinance of 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 were both passed by the Confederation Congress. They organized lands the states had ceded and are generally counted as its major success.

options.text: British efforts after the Seven Years' War to keep colonists east of the mountains and reduce frontier conflict
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: That was imperial policy in the 1760s. The ordinances encouraged American settlement in the region instead of restricting it.

options.text: The purchase of Louisiana from France, which roughly doubled the land available for farming families from the East
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Louisiana Purchase came in 1803. Thorne's township system dates to the mid-1780s and concerns the Northwest Territory.

options.text: The Missouri Compromise's division of western territory into free and slave areas along the 36 degrees 30 minutes line
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Missouri Compromise came in 1820 and dealt with the Louisiana Purchase lands. It is not the context for a policy from the 1780s.

facts: The Land Ordinance of 1785, passed by the Confederation Congress, divided western land into six-mile-square townships and reserved one section in each for public schools.
The Northwest Ordinance was enacted by the Confederation Congress in 1787 under the Articles of Confederation.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the significance of the provision on slavery mentioned in the excerpt?

options.text: It set a precedent for congressional power to bar slavery in federal territories, later cited by antislavery advocates
options.label: key
options.why: The ordinance banned slavery north of the Ohio River. Later opponents of slavery's expansion, such as the Free Soilers, pointed to it as proof that Congress could keep slavery out of the territories.

options.text: It ended slavery in all of the original states by declaring human bondage incompatible with republican government
options.label: overstated
options.why: The provision covered only the Northwest Territory. Slavery stayed legal in the Southern states, and Northern states ended it through their own gradual laws.

options.text: It applied the ban to lands south of the Ohio River, making the whole trans-Appalachian West free territory
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Southwest Territory, organized in 1790, allowed slavery. The Ohio River became a dividing line between free and slave areas, not the edge of a free West.

options.text: It led Congress to close the domestic slave trade between states, limiting slavery's growth in the early republic
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Congress banned only the international slave trade, in 1808. The domestic slave trade between states kept growing until the Civil War.

facts: The Northwest Ordinance (1787) prohibited slavery in the Northwest Territory, north of the Ohio River.
Congress banned the importation of enslaved people from abroad effective 1808, while the domestic slave trade continued.

input.title: Rotation in Office or Spoils? Two Views of Jacksonian Appointments

sources.title: Speech at a Democratic meeting, Millbrook, Pennsylvania, 1829
sources.attribution: Ezra Holloway, a wheelwright and local Jackson committee chairman, addressing a township meeting in Millbrook, Pennsylvania, 1829 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Jacksonian Democratic supporter)
sources.body: Fellow citizens, for forty years the offices of this government have been held as if they were freeholds, handed down from father to son and from patron to favorite. A clerk enters the custom house as a young man, grows gray at the same desk, and comes to believe that the public owes him his salary for life. Such men forget that they are servants. General Jackson has done no more than remind them. Let the offices circulate among the people. Any honest mechanic or farmer who can read and keep accounts is fit for most of them. A regular change keeps officeholders humble and answerable to the voters who chose the President, and it breaks up the little aristocracy that has grown up in Washington.

sources.title: Letter to a Philadelphia newspaper, 1834
sources.attribution: Nathaniel Crane, a former clerk in the Treasury Department removed from office in 1833, in a letter to a Philadelphia newspaper, 1834 (ALTON-composed, in the style of an anti-Jackson critic aligned with the emerging Whig opposition)
sources.body: I served eleven years in the Treasury and was never once asked my politics until last spring, when I was told that my place was wanted for a gentleman who had carried his ward for the administration. My successor cannot balance a ledger, but he can turn out a crowd on election day. This is what the friends of the President call reform. They have made every post office and custom house a recruiting station for the party, and every clerk a hostage to the next election. A government that pays its servants for votes rather than for work will soon have neither honest servants nor free elections. The people are not served by such a system; they are bought with their own money.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the arguments in Source A and Source B?

options.text: Source A presents rotation in office as a way to keep officials accountable to voters, while Source B presents it as a way to reward party loyalty at public expense.
options.label: key
options.why: Holloway says regular change keeps officeholders 'answerable to the voters' and breaks up an aristocracy; Crane says offices became a 'recruiting station for the party' and that people are 'bought with their own money.' This matches the real debate over Jackson's rotation in office.

options.text: Source A argues that federal offices should be reserved for educated men of property, while Source B argues that ordinary workers deserve wider access to government posts.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This flips the positions. Holloway is the one who says mechanics and farmers are fit for office, and Crane defends experienced career clerks.

options.text: Source A and Source B disagree mainly over whether the Constitution gave the President the authority to remove federal officers without Senate approval.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Removal power was debated at the time, but neither excerpt discusses constitutional authority. Both focus on whether rotation is good or bad for government.

options.text: Source A and Source B both agree that federal officeholders should be chosen chiefly for their experience, differing only on how long they should serve.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Holloway explicitly rejects long experience as a qualification and says most offices need only basic literacy and honesty, so the two do not share this premise.

facts: Andrew Jackson took office in 1829 and defended 'rotation in office,' replacing federal officeholders with his political supporters.
Critics called the practice the spoils system, a term tied to the phrase 'to the victor belong the spoils' used in Senate debate in 1832.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the argument in Source B?

options.text: A collector of the Port of New York appointed by Jackson was later found to have embezzled more than a million dollars in customs revenue.
options.label: key
options.why: Samuel Swartwout, a Jackson appointee as New York customs collector, was found in 1838 to have taken more than a million dollars. That backs Crane's claim that partisan appointees put loyalty ahead of honest, competent service.

options.text: Historians have found that Jackson removed only a minority of the federal officeholders who were serving when he took office in 1829.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Evidence that most officeholders kept their jobs would weaken Crane's claim that every post office and custom house had become a party tool. It modifies his argument instead of supporting it.

options.text: Voter turnout in presidential elections rose sharply between 1824 and 1840 as political parties organized rallies, parades, and conventions.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Turnout did rise, but more participation does not show that appointees were incompetent or corrupt. If anything, it fits Holloway's democratic framing better than Crane's.

options.text: Jackson's 1832 veto message on the Second Bank of the United States condemned government favors granted to the rich and powerful.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Bank veto is real, but it was about the Bank's charter, not about federal appointments. It says nothing about whether party appointees served honestly.

facts: Samuel Swartwout, appointed collector of the Port of New York by Jackson in 1829, was discovered in 1838 to have embezzled more than a million dollars.
Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States in 1832.

items.stem: The debate over appointments reflected in the two excerpts is best understood in the context of which broader development of the 1820s and 1830s?

options.text: The rise of mass political parties that organized a voting public enlarged by the removal of property requirements for most white men
options.label: key
options.why: Most states dropped property qualifications for white male voters by the 1830s, and the Second Party System built mass organizations. Patronage paid for party workers, and rotation in office was justified as democratic. Both excerpts belong to this context.

options.text: The fading of partisan conflict during the Era of Good Feelings, when a single national party dominated federal politics after the War of 1812
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Era of Good Feelings came before this debate and was marked by weak party competition. The excerpts show sharp partisan conflict, the opposite of that period.

options.text: The growth of reform movements, inspired by the Second Great Awakening, that tried to perfect society through temperance and moral persuasion
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Antebellum reform movements were real, but they dealt with moral and social problems, not with partisan control of federal jobs.

options.text: The rising sectional tension over whether slavery should spread into western territories after the Missouri Compromise of 1820
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Sectional tension over slavery was real, but neither excerpt mentions slavery or region. The appointments debate was about party politics and democracy.

facts: By the 1830s most states had dropped property qualifications for voting by adult white men.
The Second Party System of Democrats and Whigs took shape in the late 1820s and 1830s, using conventions, rallies, and patronage to mobilize voters.
The Missouri Compromise was enacted in 1820.

items.stem: Opposition like that in Source B to Jackson's use of presidential power most directly contributed to which development in the 1830s?

options.text: The formation of the Whig Party, which united opponents who accused Jackson of acting like a monarch
options.label: key
options.why: Anger over Jackson's use of executive power, including removals and the Bank War, brought National Republicans and other anti-Jacksonians together as the Whig Party around 1833 and 1834. The name recalled opposition to 'King Andrew.'

options.text: The Nullification Crisis, in which South Carolina declared federal tariffs void and threatened to resist federal collection
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Nullification Crisis of 1832 and 1833 grew out of the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 and states' rights theory, not out of complaints about federal appointments.

options.text: The adoption of competitive examinations to fill federal jobs, ending the practice of rewarding party workers with government posts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Merit-based civil service reform did not come until the Pendleton Act of 1883, long after the 1830s. Patronage stayed central to both parties throughout the antebellum era.

options.text: The meeting of the Hartford Convention, where New England critics of the administration proposed constitutional amendments to limit federal power
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Hartford Convention was a Federalist meeting in 1814 and 1815 during the War of 1812, well before Jackson's presidency.

facts: The Whig Party formed around 1833 and 1834 from opponents of Andrew Jackson, who mocked him as 'King Andrew I.'
The Nullification Crisis of 1832 and 1833 grew out of South Carolina's opposition to the tariffs of 1828 and 1832.
The Pendleton Civil Service Act of 1883 created merit-based examinations for some federal jobs; the Hartford Convention met in 1814 and 1815.

input.title: Slavery, Sectional Politics, and the Annexation of Texas

sources.title: A historian on the annexation of Texas
sources.attribution: Marguerite Ellison-Darrow, historian, Lone Star, Divided Union: Texas and the Politics of Expansion, a monograph from a fictional university press in Galveston, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern political history of antebellum expansion)
sources.body: Americans of the 1840s described expansion as a destiny written by Providence, but Texas shows how selective that destiny was. After Texas won its independence from Mexico in 1836, its leaders sought admission to the Union, and for nearly a decade Washington hesitated. The obstacle was not doubt about continental greatness. It was slavery. Texas would enter as a slave state, perhaps later divided into several, and Northern Whigs understood the arithmetic of the Senate. The annexation treaty of 1844 failed in the Senate after its supporters tied it openly to the protection of slavery. Only after an expansionist won the presidency that fall did Congress approve annexation in 1845, by a joint resolution needing a simple majority in each house rather than a two-thirds treaty vote. The language of Manifest Destiny did real work here: it let a measure serving slaveholding interests be presented as the fulfillment of a national mission.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?

options.text: Expansionist rhetoric about national mission helped win approval for an annexation driven mainly by the interests of slaveholders.
options.label: key
options.why: The author says the obstacle to annexation 'was slavery' and that Manifest Destiny let a measure serving slaveholding interests be presented as a national mission.

options.text: Annexation reflected a broad national agreement about continental expansion that crossed sectional lines and political parties.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author argues the reverse: the destiny was 'selective,' and Northern Whigs resisted because of slavery.

options.text: The United States delayed admitting Texas for years mainly because leaders feared that annexation would provoke a war with Great Britain.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not mention Britain. It names slavery as the obstacle.

options.text: Texas joined the Union mostly because Mexican military threats after 1836 forced the United States to protect the new republic.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author never presents Mexican threats as the cause of annexation. The passage centers on sectional politics over slavery.

facts: Texas declared and won independence from Mexico in 1836.
The Senate rejected a Texas annexation treaty in 1844, and Congress approved annexation by joint resolution in early 1845.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly modify the author's argument about the motives behind expansion in the 1840s?

options.text: James K. Polk won the 1844 election on a platform calling for both Texas and Oregon, and he carried several large Northern states.
options.label: key
options.why: Linking Texas to Oregon and winning Northern states such as New York and Pennsylvania suggests that expansion had wide appeal beyond slaveholders. That complicates the claim that slaveholding interests mainly drove it.

options.text: Northern Whigs voted in large numbers against the 1844 annexation treaty because they objected to adding another slave state.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This supports the author's argument rather than modifying it, and the excerpt already makes the point.

options.text: Many Northern opponents of slavery later backed the Wilmot Proviso to bar slavery from any land taken from Mexico.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Northern resistance to slavery's expansion fits the author's sectional reading. It does not challenge it.

options.text: Southern planters moved enslaved people into the cotton lands of eastern Texas in growing numbers during the 1830s and 1840s.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This would strengthen the claim that slaveholding interests drove annexation, so it does not modify the argument.

facts: In the 1844 election, James K. Polk ran as a Democrat favoring the annexation of Texas and claims to Oregon, and he carried Northern states including New York and Pennsylvania.
The Wilmot Proviso (1846) proposed banning slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico.

items.stem: The debate over Texas described in the excerpt is best understood as part of which broader context?

options.text: A continuing national conflict over the spread of slavery into new territories that had already flared during the Missouri crisis of 1819 to 1820
options.label: key
options.why: Northern fears about the Senate balance over Texas echoed the Missouri crisis. That crisis ended with the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which balanced slave and free states and drew a line for slavery in the Louisiana Purchase lands.

options.text: A rising nativist movement opposed to Irish and German Catholic immigrants that later produced the American, or Know-Nothing, Party of the 1850s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Nativism was real in this period, but it was not the setting for a debate centered on slavery and the balance of sectional power.

options.text: An overseas expansionist movement that ended in the annexation of Hawaii and the acquisition of the Philippines after war with Spain in 1898
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: That overseas imperialism came half a century later, in the Gilded Age and Progressive era, and had different causes.

options.text: A wave of canal and turnpike building, encouraged by state governments, that tied Western farmers to Eastern markets during the Market Revolution
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Transportation improvements were part of the era, but they do not explain a debate over adding a slave state.

facts: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state and banned slavery in the Louisiana Purchase north of 36 degrees 30 minutes, except in Missouri.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the annexation of Texas contributed to the Mexican-American War?

options.text: The United States backed the Texan claim that the Rio Grande was the border, while Mexico, which never recognized Texas independence, rejected it.
options.label: key
options.why: Mexico never accepted the loss of Texas. When Polk sent troops into the land between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande, the clash there in 1846 led to a declaration of war.

options.text: Mexico declared war at once after Texas joined the Union, because Mexican leaders believed slavery in Texas threatened their own northern provinces.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Mexico broke off diplomatic relations, but fighting began only after U.S. troops moved into the disputed border zone in 1846. The war came from the boundary dispute, not from a sudden Mexican declaration about slavery.

options.text: Congress made Texas a free state in the Compromise of 1850 to end the war, which pleased Mexico and settled the conflict over the borderlands.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Texas entered as a slave state in 1845. The Compromise of 1850 came after the war ended in 1848 and settled Texas's dispute with New Mexico over territory.

options.text: Annexation started a war with Great Britain over Oregon that pulled Mexico in as a British ally, which widened the conflict across the West.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Oregon question was settled peacefully by treaty with Britain in 1846. Britain did not ally with Mexico in a war.

facts: Fighting between U.S. and Mexican troops in the disputed area between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande in 1846 led Congress to declare war on Mexico.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) ended the war and set the Rio Grande as the Texas boundary.
The Oregon boundary dispute with Britain was settled by treaty in 1846 at the 49th parallel.

input.title: Revival and the Relocation of Religious Authority

sources.title: A historian on the Great Awakening in the Middle Colonies
sources.attribution: Miriam Adlerwood, historian, Pulpits Without Walls: Revival and Authority in the Middle Colonies, 1730-1760, published 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern scholarly monograph on colonial religion)
sources.body: When itinerant preachers rode into towns like New Brunswick and Lancaster in the early 1740s, they brought something more unsettling than a call to repentance. They invited ordinary listeners to decide for themselves whether the minister in the local pulpit was truly converted, and many listeners decided that he was not. Farmers walked out of meetinghouses where their families had sat for decades. Artisans, servants, and some enslaved people began to speak at gatherings as lay exhorters, a role once reserved for college-trained clergy. Colonial officials complained that crowds of several thousand gathered in open fields without the permission of any parish. The revival did not reject authority altogether; it moved it, from the office a man held to the spiritual experience his hearers could recognize in him. By teaching colonists to judge their leaders, the Awakening rehearsed habits of mind that would outlast the revivals themselves.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?
facts: The First Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s featured itinerant preachers who challenged the authority of established local ministers.

options.text: The revivals shifted religious authority away from formal office and training toward the judgment of ordinary believers.
options.label: key
options.why: Adlerwood says the revival 'moved' authority from 'the office a man held' to the experience hearers could recognize, and that listeners judged their own ministers.

options.text: The revivals led colonists to reject every form of religious and political authority in their communities.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author says outright that the revival 'did not reject authority altogether.'

options.text: The revivals were organized by established parish clergy who hoped to strengthen loyalty to their congregations.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt shows itinerants drawing people away from local ministers and gathering crowds without parish permission.

options.text: The revivals directly caused the colonists' decision to declare independence from Great Britain decades later.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author says only that the revival 'rehearsed habits' that lasted. She does not claim it directly caused independence.

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the 1740s would best support the argument in the excerpt?
facts: During the Great Awakening, Congregationalists split into New Lights and Old Lights, and Presbyterians split into New Side and Old Side factions.
The College of New Jersey (later Princeton) was chartered in 1746 with support from revival-minded Presbyterians.

options.text: Congregations split into pro-revival and anti-revival factions, and revival supporters set up new churches and colleges.
options.label: key
options.why: The New Light/Old Light and New Side/Old Side splits, along with new institutions like the College of New Jersey, show believers rejecting ministers they judged unconverted. That supports the claim that authority moved to the laity.

options.text: Colonial assemblies passed laws that made attending services in the established church compulsory for every free resident.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: New compulsory-attendance laws were not a feature of the 1740s. Such laws would also strengthen official authority, which is the opposite of the author's argument.

options.text: Enlightenment writers persuaded many educated colonists that reason and natural law, not revelation, revealed God's design.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Enlightenment rationalism did spread among some elites, but it says nothing about lay believers challenging the clergy's authority through revival.

options.text: The First Amendment barred Congress from establishing a national church or restricting the free exercise of religion.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The First Amendment was ratified in 1791, long after the revivals, so it cannot serve as evidence about the 1740s.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the most relevant context for the revivals described in the excerpt?
facts: George Whitefield, an English evangelical minister, toured the British North American colonies beginning in 1739, drawing large crowds.
The First Great Awakening was part of a broader evangelical revival movement across the British Atlantic world.

options.text: Evangelical Protestant revivals were spreading across the British Atlantic world, carried by touring preachers and printed sermons.
options.label: key
options.why: The colonial Awakening belonged to a transatlantic evangelical movement. Touring preachers such as George Whitefield, who arrived in 1739, and sermons spread through colonial print explain the itinerants and huge outdoor crowds.

options.text: Revivalists of the early nineteenth century were holding camp meetings on the frontier and promoting reform movements such as temperance.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes the Second Great Awakening, which came roughly two generations after the revivals in the excerpt.

options.text: Spanish missionaries were working to convert Native peoples in New Mexico and the borderlands through the mission system.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Spanish Catholic missions were real but had nothing to do with Protestant revivals in the Middle Colonies.

options.text: British victory in the Seven Years' War had removed the French threat and led to new imperial taxes on the colonies.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Seven Years' War ended in 1763, about two decades after the revivals of the early 1740s.

items.stem: The preachers described in the excerpt are best understood as emphasizing which of the following religious ideas?
facts: Great Awakening preachers such as George Whitefield and Jonathan Edwards stressed a personal, emotional conversion experience and an individual relationship with God.

options.text: Each believer needed a personal, emotional experience of conversion and a direct relationship with God.
options.label: key
options.why: Revivalists stressed heartfelt, individual conversion. That is why hearers felt able to judge whether a minister was 'truly converted.'

options.text: Human reason and observation of natural law were the surest paths to understanding God and morality.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is the rational religion and deism tied to the Enlightenment, which many revivalists opposed.

options.text: Salvation came mainly through sacraments administered by an ordained hierarchy of bishops and priests.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Revivalists put inner experience ahead of formal ritual and church hierarchy, as the excerpt's lay exhorters show.

options.text: Governments had a duty to enforce full religious toleration and separate church from state in every colony.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Some revival-era dissenters later pushed for disestablishment, but the revivals were about personal salvation, not a program requiring governments to separate church and state.

input.title: A Carpool Dispatcher's Letter During the Montgomery Bus Boycott

sources.title: Circular letter to a church congregation, Montgomery, Alabama, February 1956
sources.attribution: Letter by Odessa Pruitt, a fictional volunteer dispatcher at the Mount Gilead Chapel carpool station, read aloud and posted to the congregation, Montgomery, Alabama, February 1956 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a church circular written during the Montgomery bus boycott)
sources.body: To the members of Mount Gilead Chapel: We are now in our eleventh week off the city buses. Every morning at half past five our drivers line up their cars in the church lot, and by seven o'clock we have carried more than two hundred cooks, maids, and yardmen across town to their work. Some of our drivers have been stopped and ticketed for running what the police call an illegal taxi, and some of our people have been taken in for nothing more than waiting at a pickup corner. I ask you to meet these troubles as we have met them from the first day: without a raised fist and without a hard word. We do not walk to punish the bus company. We walk because a person who pays the same dime should not be ordered to stand so that another may sit. If the law will not yet hear us, our feet will speak, and they will speak in peace. Bring your Sunday offering for gasoline, and bring your patience.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the excerpt?
facts: The Montgomery bus boycott began in December 1955 after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat.
Boycott participants relied on volunteer carpools organized through the Montgomery Improvement Association and local churches.

options.text: To keep the congregation committed to the boycott by urging nonviolent discipline and money for the carpool system
options.label: key
options.why: Pruitt asks members to answer arrests and tickets 'without a raised fist' and to bring offerings for gasoline, aiming to sustain a peaceful boycott through its carpool network.

options.text: To persuade city officials to settle the dispute by hiring African American drivers for routes in Black neighborhoods
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter is addressed to church members, not officials, and makes no hiring demand.

options.text: To call on members of Congress to pass a federal law banning racial segregation on buses that cross state lines
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter never mentions Congress or federal legislation; its audience and request are local.

options.text: To encourage church members to defend themselves with force against police who arrested carpool drivers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author explicitly rejects any 'raised fist' and asks for a peaceful response to arrests.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the argument the author makes in the excerpt?
facts: Montgomery city bus rules in 1955 required African American riders to give up seats to white riders when ordered by drivers.

options.text: Segregated seating is unjust because equal fares deserve equal treatment, and peaceful refusal to ride is a proper response
options.label: key
options.why: The author says a person 'who pays the same dime' should not have to stand for another and that 'our feet will speak' in peace.

options.text: The boycott should continue until the bus company is driven out of business as punishment for its discriminatory treatment
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author states directly, 'We do not walk to punish the bus company.'

options.text: Lawsuits in the federal courts offer the only reliable way to end segregation, so the protest walking should soon be ended
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author suggests the law 'will not yet hear us' and treats walking as the response, not something to abandon.

options.text: Separate seating could be acceptable if the city provided more buses and better service to African American neighborhoods
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author objects to being ordered to stand for another rider, a challenge to segregation itself, not a request for better separate service.

items.stem: The boycott described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following?
facts: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court ruled that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional.
African Americans in the 1950s increasingly combined court challenges with local organized protest against Jim Crow laws.

options.text: A growing postwar challenge to Jim Crow, as African Americans encouraged by rulings such as Brown v. Board of Education organized local protests
options.label: key
options.why: The 1955-1956 boycott came soon after the 1954 Brown decision, part of a wider 1950s movement that pressed against segregation both in court and through community action.

options.text: The first large wave of the Great Migration, as African Americans left the rural South for industrial jobs in northern cities during the First World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The first Great Migration wave came in the 1910s; the excerpt shows Southerners resisting segregation in a Southern city in the 1950s.

options.text: Enforcement of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as federal officials began bringing lawsuits against Southern cities that kept segregated public facilities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Civil Rights Act was passed eight years after the events of the letter.

options.text: The Black Power movement, which stressed racial pride, community self-defense, and doubts about whether integration should be the main goal of activists
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Black Power emerged in the mid-to-late 1960s, and its emphasis on self-defense differs from the letter's strict nonviolence.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments most directly built on the methods described in the excerpt?
facts: Beginning in February 1960, college students in Greensboro, North Carolina, staged sit-ins at a segregated lunch counter, and the tactic spread across the South.
The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was founded in 1960.
President Eisenhower sent federal troops to Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1957 to enforce school desegregation.

options.text: Student sit-ins that began at Greensboro lunch counters in 1960 and spread across the South, using disciplined nonviolent protest to confront segregation
options.label: key
options.why: The sit-ins and the founding of SNCC in 1960 extended the boycott's organized, nonviolent mass action against segregated public places.

options.text: President Eisenhower's decision to send federal troops to Montgomery in 1957 to protect African American riders on newly desegregated buses
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Eisenhower sent troops to Little Rock in 1957 to enforce school desegregation, not to Montgomery for bus riders.

options.text: The passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 as a direct result of the boycott's victory over segregated buses in Montgomery
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Voting Rights Act followed later voting campaigns such as Selma in 1965; describing it as a direct result of the bus boycott is an overstatement.

options.text: A decision by Southern civil rights groups to give up mass protest and rely only on lawsuits after the boycott came to an end
options.label: reversal
options.why: After the boycott, groups such as SCLC, founded in 1957, increased their use of mass nonviolent protest rather than giving it up.

input.title: The Harlem Renaissance and Its Paying Public

sources.title: A historian on the foundations of the Harlem Renaissance
sources.attribution: Theodora V. Mapes, historian, Harlem's Paying Public: Audience and Institution in the New Negro Movement, a fictional monograph, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a scholarly monograph)
sources.body: For decades, accounts of the Harlem Renaissance opened in the drawing rooms of wealthy white patrons and the offices of downtown publishers. That vantage point mistakes the sponsors for the foundation. The movement rested first on a Black urban public that had not existed a generation earlier. Between the First World War and the late 1920s, hundreds of thousands of Southern migrants settled in Northern cities, and Harlem became their best-known destination. These newcomers bought the race newspapers, filled the cabarets and churches, and paid admission to the rent parties where pianists tried out new styles of jazz and blues. Black-run institutions mattered just as much. The magazines of the NAACP and the National Urban League printed young poets and, in the mid-1920s, offered literary prizes that introduced new talent to the nation. When the Depression emptied Harlem's pockets after 1929, the movement faltered, not because patrons lost interest, but because its home audience could no longer pay.

items.stem: Which of the following does the author use as evidence that the Harlem Renaissance depended on institutions run by African Americans?

options.text: Literary prizes offered by the magazines of national civil rights and racial uplift organizations
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt cites the magazines of the NAACP and the National Urban League, which published young poets and sponsored literary prizes in the mid-1920s, as Black-run institutions that sustained the movement.

options.text: Financial support that wealthy white patrons gave to promising Black poets, novelists, and painters
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author explicitly argues that patrons were sponsors rather than the foundation, so this is the view the excerpt argues against.

options.text: Federal relief programs that paid Black writers and artists to produce guidebooks, murals, and plays
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: New Deal arts programs such as the Federal Writers' Project began in 1935, after the period the author describes, and the excerpt never mentions them.

options.text: Commercial radio networks that carried jazz performances from Harlem nightclubs to listeners across the nation
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Radio did spread jazz in the 1920s, but the author points to rent parties, cabarets, and magazines, not radio, as evidence.

facts: The NAACP published The Crisis, and the National Urban League published Opportunity, both of which promoted Black writers in the 1920s.
Opportunity and The Crisis sponsored literary contests in the mid-1920s, including 1925.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most challenge the author's explanation for why the Harlem Renaissance faltered in the 1930s?

options.text: Evidence that white-owned publishers stopped accepting Black authors' work while Harlem readers kept buying books and magazines
options.label: key
options.why: The author says the movement declined because its home audience could no longer pay, not because sponsors withdrew. If Harlem demand held steady while publishers pulled back, the cause would lie with downtown sponsors, which would undercut her argument.

options.text: Evidence that unemployment and poverty in Harlem rose sharply in the first years of the Great Depression
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rising hardship in Harlem would back up the author's claim that the local audience could no longer afford cultural products.

options.text: Evidence that most migrants to Northern cities came from the rural South looking for industrial wages
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate about the Great Migration, but it explains where the audience came from, not why the movement declined.

options.text: Evidence that the NAACP's magazine kept publishing poetry and essays throughout the 1930s
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: One magazine continuing to publish says little about whether patrons or the local audience caused the broader decline.

facts: The Great Depression began after the stock market crash of 1929 and hit African American communities such as Harlem especially hard.
The Crisis continued publication through the 1930s.

items.stem: The growth of the Black urban public described in the excerpt resulted most directly from which of the following developments?

options.text: African Americans moving from the South to Northern cities for wartime industrial jobs and to escape Jim Crow
options.label: key
options.why: The Great Migration, which sped up during the First World War as labor demand rose and European immigration fell, created the urban Black communities, Harlem among them, that the author describes.

options.text: Black families leaving the drought-stricken Plains for California in search of agricultural work
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Dust Bowl migration came in the 1930s, mostly involved white Plains farmers, and headed west, not to Northern cities.

options.text: Formerly enslaved people settling in Kansas to farm homesteads after Reconstruction ended
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Exoduster movement of 1879 was a rural migration in Period 6, not the urban migration around the First World War.

options.text: Southern Black workers moving to West Coast shipyards and defense plants during the Second World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This second wave of the Great Migration in the 1940s came after the 1920s growth of Harlem described in the excerpt.

facts: The Great Migration of African Americans from the South to Northern cities accelerated during World War I (1914-1918) because of industrial labor demand.
The Exoduster migration to Kansas took place mainly in 1879.

items.stem: The cultural movement described in the excerpt most directly anticipated which of the following later developments?

options.text: The emphasis on Black pride, heritage, and self-defined identity that marked the Black Power movement in the late 1960s
options.label: key
options.why: The New Negro ideal of the Harlem Renaissance celebrated African American culture and identity. That emphasis on racial pride returned in the cultural side of Black Power and the Black Arts Movement in the late 1960s.

options.text: The Supreme Court's 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling, which writers of the Harlem Renaissance had argued for in court
options.label: overstated
options.why: Brown came from decades of NAACP legal work led by lawyers, not from Renaissance literature; saying the movement directly produced the ruling overstates the connection.

options.text: The emphasis on industrial education and accommodation to segregation that civil rights groups adopted in the 1950s
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Accommodation and industrial education are tied to Booker T. Washington in the 1890s, and civil rights groups of the 1950s rejected accommodation instead of adopting it.

options.text: Marcus Garvey's founding of a mass movement calling for Black pride and economic independence among urban migrants
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association was active in Harlem at the same time as the Renaissance, so it was not a later development the Renaissance anticipated.

facts: The Black Power movement of the late 1960s emphasized racial pride and African American cultural identity.
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) resulted from the NAACP's legal strategy against school segregation.
Marcus Garvey's UNIA was based in Harlem and at its height in the early 1920s.

input.title: A Kansas Lumber Dealer Argues for Cutting Income Tax Rates, 1981

sources.title: Remarks to a Merchants' Association
sources.attribution: Harlan Veatch, owner of a lumberyard, speech to the Ashby Merchants' Association, Ashby, Kansas, March 1981; Veatch is a fictional speaker (ALTON-composed, in the style of a small-business owner's civic club address)
sources.body: Friends, I have kept the books for this lumberyard for twenty-two years, and I have never seen a decade like the one just ended. Prices doubled while my sales stood still. Every time I gave my yardmen a raise to keep up with the grocery bill, Washington pushed them into a higher bracket, and they took home less than before. Nobody ever voted for that tax increase. Now the new administration proposes to cut income tax rates across the board over three years. Some in Congress call it a giveaway to the rich. I call it letting a man keep what he earns. When I keep more, I hire another driver, I buy a second truck, I extend credit to the young couple building on Elm Street. Lower rates will mean more work done, and more work done will mean more revenue for the Treasury, not less. So write to our congressman. The question is simple: do we trust the people who earn the money, or the bureaus that spend it?

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of Veatch's remarks?

options.text: To build local pressure on Congress to pass the administration's proposed income tax rate cuts
options.label: key
options.why: Veatch defends the three-year across-the-board rate cut proposed by the new Reagan administration in early 1981 and tells his audience to write their congressman, showing his aim is to rally support for its passage.

options.text: To warn local merchants that federal tax cuts would produce budget deficits and higher interest rates
options.label: reversal
options.why: Veatch claims lower rates will raise revenue; he does not warn about deficits. That concern came from the plan's critics.

options.text: To persuade the merchants to support higher tariffs protecting American lumber from foreign competition
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The speech says nothing about trade or tariffs. It deals only with income tax rates and bracket creep.

options.text: To urge the merchants to back new federal programs that would raise wages to keep pace with inflation
options.label: reversal
options.why: Veatch distrusts the federal bureaus that spend tax money and wants less government, not new federal wage programs.

facts: In early 1981 the Reagan administration proposed cutting individual income tax rates across the board over three years.
Congress passed the Economic Recovery Tax Act in 1981, cutting individual income tax rates by about 25 percent over three years.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Veatch's main argument about lowering income tax rates?

options.text: Lower rates would spur enough investment and hiring that government revenue would actually rise
options.label: key
options.why: Veatch says he would hire workers and buy equipment with his tax savings, and that more work done means more revenue, not less. That is the core supply-side argument behind Reagan-era tax policy.

options.text: Lower rates for working people should be paid for by shifting more of the tax burden onto large corporations
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Veatch never proposes shifting taxes onto corporations. He wants rates cut across the board.

options.text: Lower rates could only be justified after Congress first made deep and lasting cuts to federal spending
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Veatch criticizes the bureaus that spend money, but he does not make spending cuts a condition for cutting taxes. He expects growth to replace the lost revenue.

options.text: Lower rates mattered less than breaking the power of labor unions, which he blamed for driving up prices
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The speech mentions inflation and his workers' raises but blames federal tax brackets, not unions, for workers' losses.

facts: Supply-side economics, influential in the Reagan administration, held that lower marginal tax rates would encourage work, saving and investment and could offset revenue losses through growth.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the most direct context for the economic complaints Veatch describes?

options.text: The combination of high inflation and slow growth in the 1970s that pushed rising wages into higher tax brackets
options.label: key
options.why: Veatch describes prices doubling while sales stagnated and raises pushing workers into higher brackets. This was the stagflation and bracket creep of the 1970s that fueled demand for tax cuts.

options.text: The financial crisis and severe recession of 2007 to 2009, which led to bank failures and high unemployment
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The speech dates from 1981 and looks back on the decade just ended, the 1970s, not the Great Recession decades later.

options.text: The rapid economic growth and suburban prosperity of the 1950s, which raised incomes and federal revenues
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Veatch describes stagnant sales and rising prices, not postwar prosperity, and his speech refers to the 1970s.

options.text: The reductions in military spending after the Cold War ended, which freed federal funds for tax relief
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Cold War ended around 1989 to 1991, after this 1981 speech, and defense spending actually grew in the early 1980s.

facts: The 1970s saw stagflation, a combination of high inflation and slow economic growth, worsened by the oil shocks of 1973 and 1979.
Before income tax brackets were indexed to inflation, rising nominal wages pushed taxpayers into higher brackets ('bracket creep').

items.stem: Which of the following was a significant result of the tax policies Veatch supported, combined with other federal policies of the 1980s?

options.text: Federal budget deficits and the national debt grew sharply as tax cuts coincided with a large military buildup
options.label: key
options.why: The 1981 rate cuts reduced revenue while the Reagan administration greatly increased defense spending. Large annual deficits followed, and the national debt roughly tripled during the decade, undercutting Veatch's prediction about revenue.

options.text: The federal government ran balanced budgets for most of the decade because growth fully replaced the lost tax revenue
options.label: reversal
options.why: The budget was not balanced in the 1980s. Surpluses did not appear until the late 1990s.

options.text: Income inequality narrowed noticeably because tax savings were spread evenly among wage earners and the wealthy
options.label: reversal
options.why: Income inequality widened during the 1980s, and the largest benefits of the rate cuts went to higher earners.

options.text: Military spending fell steadily during the decade as the administration moved resources toward domestic programs
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Reagan administration expanded defense spending and tried to reduce domestic social spending, the opposite of this claim.

facts: Federal budget deficits rose sharply in the 1980s, and the national debt roughly tripled between 1981 and 1989.
The Reagan administration carried out a major military buildup during the 1980s.
